units.title: 4. Exam Preparation
units.description: Model questions from Section A and B.

slides.title: Section A (2 Marks) — Point of View
slides.content:
**Question:** Analyse the relevance of the point of view employed in Chiang's story. Is it a common point of view employed by writers?

**Model Answer:** Chiang employs a **second-person point of view** ('you') combined with a narrator from the future. This is unusual and effective because it directly implicates the reader in the story's warning about free will. Unlike the more common first or third person, this POV creates an **immediate sense of urgency** and blurs the boundary between fiction and reality, making the philosophical message more personally impactful.

slides.title: Section B (6 Marks) — What does the Predictor symbolise?
slides.content:
**Question:** What does the 'Predictor' in Ted Chiang's story symbolise?

**Model Answer:**
1. **Technological determinism** — modern devices anticipate our needs before we know them.
2. **Smartphones and social media** — addictive gadgets that control behaviour.
3. **Social constructs** — choices imposed on individuals without their awareness.
4. **A human face** (green LED smile) — relationships built without critical questioning.
5. **Gradual erosion of free will** — the tragic self-deception becoming a way of life.

The description of the device's 'heart' as consisting of circuits further points to the human-machine resemblance.

slides.title: Exam Practice
slides.question: Why does the narrator from the future say 'Because I had no choice' at the end of the story?

options.text: The narrator was forced by others to send the warning.
It demonstrates the paradox — even sending the warning was predetermined by a deterministic universe.
options.explanation: The ending is a self-referential paradox: if free will is an illusion, then sending the warning itself was predetermined, making the act futile and inevitable simultaneously.

options.text: The narrator lacked the technology to stop sending it.
The narrator wanted to prove free will exists.
options.explanation: The narrator acknowledges free will is an illusion throughout.
